newsitem.title: BOSNIA: US says Serbs to fire cops - war crimes suspects.
newsitem.headline: US says Serbs to fire cops - war crimes suspects.

text.p: Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic has promised to sack four policemen indicted by the international war crimes tribunal on former Yugoslavia (ICTY), a senior U.S. official said on Monday.

But John Shattuck, U.S. assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, said Plavsic baulked at handing over the four and other Serb indictees to the tribunal in The Hague for trial.
Shattuck was briefing reporters midway through four days of talks with Serb, Moslem and Croat leaders on unfulfilled human rights provisions of the 1995 Dayton peace treaty on Bosnia.
He said he warned Serb and Croat representatives in particular that continued disregard of their commitment to relinquish war-crimes indictees would cost them vital reconstruction aid from the West.

"I received a commitment from (Plavsic) that the four individuals now serving in the police department in Prijedor will be fired," Shattuck said when asked what his meeting with the nationalist Bosnian Serb president on Sunday produced.
"I indicated to her that this was not sufficient, that they and other indicted war criminals must be brought to justice in The Hague ... (But Plavsic made) very insufficient guarantees.
"I made clear to her that if there were not better guarantees there would be negative political and economic consequences," the U.S. human rights supremo said.
Plavsic had argued that the Serb republic's constitution ruled out extradition of its citizens abroad but Shattuck said this was no excuse for ignoring international law.

Shattuck said he drove similar points home in talks with Bosnian Croat leader Kresimir Zubak. Croats control part of a shaky federation with Moslems that covers half of Bosnia. The other half is a Bosnian Serb Republic.
The four Prijedor policemen were indicted for atrocities against Moslem prisoners in several notorious detention camps run in the Serb-held north at the start of the war in 1992.
Shattuck said he also raised the case of five Serb indictees believed to be living openly -- and possibly in two cases holding public office -- in Bosanski Samac.

He took Zubak to task for failure to round up two major Croat war-crimes suspects -- Dario Kordic, former head of the Bosnian wing of Croatia's ruling party, and Ivica Rajic, an ex- militia commander.
Kordic and Rajic are both accused of complicity in massacres of Moslem civilians in central Bosnia.

Croatia armed Bosnian Croats in their 1993-94 separatist war and is deemed co-responsible by the West for extradition of Croat indictees. Shattuck said he would meet Croatian President Franjo Tudjman about the issue on Tuesday.

Shattuck will go to Belgrade on Wednesday to lean on President Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia for cooperation with the tribunal as well. He has ignored repeated demands to extradite ex-Yugoslav army officers indicted for massacres of Croats in Croatia's 1991 war for independence from federal Yugoslavia.

Over two thirds of the 75 tribunal indictees are Serbs, including wartime political leader Radovan Karadzic and army chief General Ratko Mladic, while 18 are Croats. Less than 10 are in custody, most of them arrested in Western Europe.

Asked how he could expect the parties to be more responsive this time unless the NATO peace force in Bosnia, whose mandate is now being re-defined by alliance planners, were empowered to hunt down indicted war criminals, he said:
"I'm not here to discuss future mandates of particular (international) security forces but you are well aware there are discussions under way on that subject now.
"This is ... a time when we are entering a new phase of the implementation of the peace process, so for that reason the urgency of compliance is being underscored more than ever."
